quote: Welches sind nun die Fixpunkte der Substitution?
english: What, now, are the fixed points of the substitution?
topic: Hilbert considers a function f of the coefficients u_ik of a quadratic form ψ, defined as an infinite sum of 1/ψ^s over all integer vectors, and plans to study its invariance substitutions, a fundamental domain in complex u-space, and the fixed points of the substitutions, beginning with the case n = 3.

triage.modern_statement: Hilbert's sum is what is now called the Epstein zeta function, Z(u;s) = Σ_{x∈Z^n, x≠0} ψ_u(x)^(-s), where ψ_u(x) = Σ u_ik x_i x_k. Because the sum runs over all of Z^n, it does not change under the unimodular substitutions u ↦ AᵀuA with A ∈ GL(n,Z). The question asks for the fixed points of this action: which symmetric matrices u (real positive-definite, or complex where the series converges) satisfy AᵀuA = λu, or AᵀuA = u, for some A ≠ ±I? Put another way: which forms have a nontrivial integral automorphism group, and what are the elliptic or branch points of the fundamental domain for GL(n,Z), starting with n = 3? I am inferring this framing from the page summary. The surviving note is only the one-line question.
triage.answered_by: No single person answered it. For real positive-definite forms, the answer is the classical theory of forms (lattices) with nontrivial automorphism groups, and Hilbert's case n = 3 is the classification into the 14 Bravais lattice types. In that theory, Bravais types correspond one-to-one to conjugacy classes of certain finite subgroups of GL_n(Z). This is set out, for example, in the Plesken–Hanrath paper on 6-dimensional lattices (Math. Comp. 43, 1984), which extends the classical classification. The closest complex analogue is the Siegel upper half-space with Sp(2n,Z) acting on it. There E. Gottschling worked out the fixed points and fixed-point subgroups of the degree-2 Siegel modular group (1959–61), and Siegel and Gottschling built the fundamental domain. I found no source that names Hilbert's diary question directly, so these links are my own identification.

evidence.claim: The Epstein zeta function is defined from a positive-definite quadratic form given by a positive-definite symmetric matrix A in n variables, which matches the object Hilbert describes.

Bravais types of lattices correspond one-to-one with conjugacy classes of certain finite subgroups of GL_n(Z), the Bravais classification by automorphism groups. These are the forms fixed by nontrivial unimodular substitutions.
The 3-dimensional Bravais lattice groups are characterized as maximal finite subgroups of GL(3,Z).
Gottschling computed the fixed points and fixed-point subgroups of Sp(2,Z) (1961), in connection with the Siegel–Gottschling fundamental domain.
Gottschling's classification of fixed points of the Siegel modular group is still cited and used today, for example in physics models built on modular invariance.

The question is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. Read in modern terms, it is about forms with nontrivial unimodular automorphisms, or elliptic fixed points of an arithmetic group on a symmetric space. For real forms, especially n = 3 (the Bravais classification), that is classical, settled mathematics. For the complex setting, Siegel and Gottschling's work on fixed points of the Siegel modular group (1959–61) is the closest settled analogue. The broader subject is still used, but this particular question is not an open research problem. Because it is unclear exactly which substitution group and which complex domain Hilbert meant, my confidence is low.
